content:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it's going to be recorded for research purposes, so just bear that in mind.

The main thing I want to say before we get going is that this is genuinely a conversation — between all of you — rather than me firing questions at you one by one. So if something someone else says connects with your experience, or you disagree with it, please just jump in. You don't need to wait to be asked. There's no right or wrong answer to anything we're going to talk about, and I'm not looking for a particular view — I'm just interested in what you actually think and what you've actually experienced. Honest and specific is much more useful to me than polished.

I won't be sharing my own opinions on any of this — my job is just to keep things moving and make sure everyone gets a chance to speak. So if I come back to you with a follow-up question, it's because I'm genuinely curious, not because you said something wrong.

Okay, let's get started. Let's go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
Right, yeah. I'm Bilal, I'm from Leeds — so Yorkshire and Humber. I'm 32. Thanks for having us all here.
Noah, I'm from Lisburn, so Northern Ireland — suburban area just outside Belfast. I'm 32 as well. Cheers for having us.
Yeah, cheers. I'm Connor, I'm 34, and I'm from London — Greater London, so urban area. Bit different from you two with the commute and everything, but yeah, good to be here.
I'm Sam, I'm 33, from the South West — suburban area, so I reckon I'm somewhere in the middle of you lot in terms of the setup. Yeah, good to be here.

Right, yeah, I'm Henry. I'm 35, and I'm from Birmingham — so Urban West Midlands. I know what you mean, Connor, about the commute being different. I've got mates in London and it's just a whole other thing, innit. Getting around the city here is nothing like that. But I reckon all of us who are in cities probably deal with some of the same stuff — just different scales maybe. Good to be here as well.

Great, good to have everyone here — Birmingham, Leeds, Belfast, London, South West. Nice spread. Right, let's get into it. First thing I want to ask is: what's your favourite place in your city or town to spend time with your male friends? Can be anywhere — a pub, a park, someone's house, wherever. And why that place specifically?

Yeah, for me it's probably the pub, to be honest. There's a few we go to round town — nothing fancy, just local spots where you know the staff and people recognise you. That's the thing about it, innit. You can just show up, have a pint, chat about whatever's going on. No pressure to do anything special. It's just easy.

Yeah, that's exactly it for me too. We've got a couple of spots in Lisburn like that — one near the town centre where half the people you see on a Saturday night you've either worked with or gone to school with. That recognition thing Bilal's talking about, it's... it just takes the edge off, doesn't it? You're not performing or anything. You can just be there.

I reckon in a place like this though, there's maybe a bit more of that going on than in a bigger city where you're more anonymous. Like, everyone knows everyone to some degree, so the pub becomes the place where that's just normal and accepted. You're not trying to impress anyone because they already know you.

Yeah, I get that — but I'd say Leeds is pretty big, and I still get that same thing, you know? If you find your spot, even in a city, you're not anonymous. It's the same crew most nights. People know you. I think it's more about finding the right pub than the size of the place, if that makes sense. Like, there's definitely pubs in Leeds where you're just a face in the crowd, but the ones we go to, we're regulars. It's the same vibe you're describing, Noah.

Fair point, yeah. I was maybe oversimplifying it a bit. You're right — it's not really about the place being small or big, it's about being a regular somewhere. That's the thing that matters. Leeds is a city but if you've got your spots and you're in them enough, you're known. Same outcome either way.

Yeah, I'd agree with that. I've got a couple of pubs in Birmingham where I'm pretty much a regular — same faces, you know the staff, they know what you drink. That's always been the thing for me too. But I'll be honest, it's gotten a bit harder to maintain that these days. Like, I used to go to one spot every Friday without fail, but life just gets in the way — work's different, mates move, people have kids. You miss a few weeks and suddenly you're not a regular anymore, you're just... a bloke who comes in sometimes.

So yeah, Bilal's right — it's less about the size of the city and more about actually being there regularly. But it takes effort to keep it going, doesn't it? Not saying it's a big problem or anything, just it's not as automatic as it used to be.
Sam, you've been quiet — whereabouts in the South West are you, and have you got places like that where you'd go with mates?

Yeah, I'm in a suburban area, so it's a bit more spread out than what you're all describing really. There's a few pubs near me, but I wouldn't say I'm a regular in the same way you lot are talking about. It's more... I'll meet mates at one place one week, somewhere else another time, depending on who's around and what they fancy. Less of a "that's my spot" thing, I reckon.

That said, there's definitely a pub closer to home where I'll bump into people I know — not every week necessarily, but enough that the staff recognise me. There's something to what Henry said about it getting harder to keep up as life moves on. I get that. You've got work, family stuff, it's not always easy to just pick the same place every Friday like you used to.

But honestly, I don't think I mind it as much. I'm pretty happy just going where suits, really. Doesn't feel like something I'm missing out on by not being a proper regular somewhere.
Connor, what about you — London's a different animal. Have you got somewhere you'd go with mates, or does it work differently there?

Yeah, I mean... it's a bit like what Sam said, to be honest. London's just massive, innit. I've got mates scattered all over the place — some in zone one, some further out — so it's never really been the same pub every week thing for me. We'll just pick somewhere that's roughly in the middle or near where someone's working that day. There's definitely pubs I go to more than others, but I wouldn't call myself a regular in the way you lot are describing. It's more practical than anything else.

I think if I lived somewhere smaller I might have that, but the geography just doesn't really lend itself to it. By the time you've worked out where everyone can actually get to without spending an hour on the tube, you've kind of accepted you're going to rotate spots, you know? So I don't really feel like I'm missing out or anything. It's just how it works.

Cheers Connor. So it sounds like whether it's Leeds or Lisburn or London, it's less about having one fixed spot and more about what works given who you're with and where you all are. Good stuff. Let's shift gears slightly — thinking now about food rather than where you go. How do you decide what to eat? Day to day, week to week — what's actually driving those choices?

For me it's pretty straightforward, really. I eat meat most days — couple times a week red meat, couple times poultry. I'll have fish maybe once a month or so. And eggs pretty much every day, dairy as well. 

Honestly, it's just what I've always done. I don't think about it that much. It's convenient, it's what I grew up eating, and I enjoy it. I'll have a curry, a steak, some chicken — it's just normal to me. I'm not like... militant about it or anything. I just eat what I fancy and what's available. That's sort of it.

Yeah, I'm pretty similar to you, Bilal, in terms of what I actually eat — meat most days, not thinking about it too much. But I'll be honest, I reckon I do think about it a bit more than I used to. Not in like a preachy way or anything, just... as you get older, you start noticing these things, don't you? 

Like, I used to just grab whatever was quickest or cheapest without really considering it. Now I'm in my mid-30s, and I do find myself thinking about it a bit more — where stuff comes from, whether I'm eating the same thing too often. Nothing dramatic, just different from when I was 25 and just ate whatever was put in front of me.

I'm still eating meat, still having red meat once a week, chicken regularly, all that. But yeah, it's not quite as automatic as it was for me. I reckon that's just part of getting older though, isn't it — you start paying attention to stuff you didn't before.

Yeah, that's... actually fair. I know what you mean. I'm the same age as you and I do notice that happening, even if I don't make a massive deal out of it. You just become a bit more aware of things without really deciding to, you know? 

I wouldn't say I'm constantly thinking about where my food comes from or anything like that, but yeah — there's moments where you're in the supermarket or ordering something and you just... clock it a bit more than you used to. It's not like I'm changing what I eat because of it, but the awareness is definitely there in a way it wasn't when I was younger.

I think you're right that it's just part of getting older. You pay attention to more stuff without meaning to.

Yeah, exactly — you're clocking it without necessarily doing anything about it yet. But I wonder if that's the thing, innit. Like, once you've clocked it, you can't really unclok it. Even if you're not changing what you eat right now, that awareness is just sitting there. 

I'm not saying it means we'll both become vegetarian or anything — I genuinely don't know. But it does feel different from before, when you just weren't thinking about it at all. Now it's like, you're aware the choice exists, even if you're still making the same choice you always did.

That's probably why it feels a bit different to when we were younger and just ate without thinking. You can't really go back to not thinking about it once you've started, can you? Whether that leads somewhere or just stays as awareness, I'm not sure yet. But it's definitely a shift.

Yeah, that's the thing though, isn't it? You can't unknow something. Once you're aware of it, it's just... there. But I'm not sure that means you have to do anything about it, if that makes sense. Like, I'm aware of loads of things — aware I could exercise more, aware I could probably eat less processed stuff, whatever. But being aware and actually changing something are two different things.

With food, I just... I don't feel like I'm under pressure to change because I've clocked something. It's more like, I notice it, and then I just carry on. I still eat the same because that's what works for me day to day. The awareness doesn't necessarily pull me in any direction, you know? It's just sitting there, like you said. And that's fine. I'm okay with that.

That distinction between noticing something and feeling like you have to act on it — that's interesting. Sam, Noah, Connor — how does that land with you? And more broadly, what's actually driving what you eat day to day?

I think... yeah, I get what you're both saying, but I reckon there's maybe a difference between just being aware of something and when it actually hits you in a moment, you know? 

Like, I eat meat regularly, same as Bilal and Henry — chicken most days, red meat once a week, that sort of thing. And I'm not sitting around thinking about it constantly or anything. But there are these odd moments where you're standing in the supermarket or ordering something, and you just... feel it a bit differently than you normally would. Not enough to make me change what I'm buying, necessarily, but it's there.

It's almost like — being aware in general is one thing. But then there's these specific moments where the awareness actually lands in a way that makes you pause for a second. And I think those are different things. You can know something intellectually and not really feel it, but then something will just catch you on a particular day and it shifts how you feel about the choice, even if you're still making the same choice.

That's probably closer to what I experience day to day, I reckon. Not constant pressure or anything, just these moments where it's not quite as automatic as Bilal's describing.

Yeah, okay — fair point. I think I was maybe making it sound simpler than it actually is. Connor's right, there are those moments, aren't there? Like, you do sometimes just... pause. You're buying something or you see something and it just lands different for a second.

I wouldn't have said that was happening to me before, but thinking about it now, yeah — there are times when it's not quite automatic. It's not like I'm wrestling with it or anything, but it's not quite as straightforward as just picking what I fancy either. There's a little something there that wasn't there before.

I think I was trying to not make it into a big thing, but you're right — it's probably worth acknowledging that it's not as simple as I first made it sound. It's just not... I don't know, it doesn't feel like it's pushing me towards any particular decision yet. It's just a bit more complicated than I was saying.

Yeah, that idea of it being a bit more complicated than it first appears — that's come through from a few of you. Let's move on to something that sits underneath all of this. Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Whether that's the stuff you choose, how you feel about certain foods, what you'd order in front of other people — anything like that.

I mean... yeah, I reckon it probably does, if I'm being honest. Though it's not something I sit around thinking about day to day, you know?

Like, I eat meat — chicken, red meat — and I think there's probably an assumption in there somewhere that that's just what I do. What men do. I don't know if it's something I picked up growing up or if it's just... the culture, or whatever. But when I'm at the supermarket or ordering something, red meat or chicken feels normal to me in a way that... I don't know. I just don't see myself ordering a salad or something vegetarian in front of my mates. That would feel a bit off.

I'm not saying my mates would give me grief about it or anything — I don't think they would. But there's something there, isn't there? Some part of you that just assumes meat is the thing, especially if you're a bloke. It's hard to explain without sounding a bit daft, but yeah. I think gender's in there somewhere, even if I'm not actively thinking about it.

I genuinely don't know if that's something I'd change or if it's just... how it is. But the moderator's asking if it influences me, and I reckon the answer's probably yeah, it does.

Yeah, I know exactly what you mean, Sam. And I think it's... it's a bit mad when you actually name it, but it's definitely there. Like, you're right — nobody's going to give you shit for it, but there's this invisible thing, isn't there?

In Northern Ireland especially, I reckon that's quite strong. There's just this assumption that meat is what you do. You're a bloke, you eat meat. It's not like anyone's sitting you down and telling you that explicitly, but it's just... in the air somehow. And I do think I feel it, even though I wouldn't say I'm bothered about it or anything. Like, if I decided to go vegetarian tomorrow, I'm pretty sure my mates wouldn't actually care. But there's still this part of you that thinks... that's not what we do, you know?

The thing that gets me though is how much of a thing people make it when it does come up. Like, if someone mentions they're vegetarian or they're thinking about cutting back on meat, suddenly it becomes this whole conversation. People get defensive about it in a way that's kind of bizarre, honestly. It's like the assumption itself is so strong that questioning it feels threatening somehow. And that bothers me a bit — the reaction says more than the original choice does, I reckon.

Yeah, that's... yeah, I know what you mean. You're right about that defensive thing. I've seen that happen loads of times — someone says they're cutting back or they've gone veggie, and suddenly everyone's got an opinion about it, or they're making jokes, or... it just becomes this whole thing. And you're right, Noah — it does say something, doesn't it? Like, if it was just a normal choice, nobody would care. But the fact that people get defensive about it, or feel like they need to defend themselves for eating meat — that's weird when you actually clock it.

And I think you've kind of hit on why I feel that pull, actually. It's not really that my mates would judge me for ordering something vegetarian. It's more like... I've probably picked up on that defensiveness without even noticing I was doing it. Like, it's so embedded in how we all talk about food that you just absorb it, you know? And then you're kind of avoiding something that hasn't even been said yet.

That's different from what I was saying before, I reckon. It's not about my choice — it's about how loaded the whole thing is. Once you've seen how defensive people get about it, you just... you don't want to be the thing that sets that off, even if logically you know it shouldn't matter.

Exactly — that's it, really. You're dodging something that nobody's even asked you to dodge yet. And in a place like Lisburn, that stuff gets really entrenched because everyone knows everyone, doesn't it? Like, if someone goes vegetarian, it's not just a personal choice — it becomes a thing people talk about. And you can feel that anticipation before it even happens.

I've seen it happen with mates. Someone says they're thinking about cutting back on red meat for whatever reason — health, cost, just doesn't fancy it — and you watch people scramble to defend themselves. And it's like, nobody's attacking you, but there's this instant reflex to justify why they're still eating it. As if they've been accused of something.

The weird part is, I don't actually care that much either way. Like, meat, no meat — it doesn't bother me. But I can see how that defensiveness becomes self-perpetuating, you know? Because once it's that loaded, even someone who genuinely might be open to it thinks, "I'm not getting into that" and just keeps eating what they've always eaten. And then the whole thing stays exactly as it is. 

It's a bit embarrassing when you think about it, honestly. The fact that we've made it into something where people have to defend a dietary choice at all. That's not really about food, is it?

Noah's putting his finger on something there — this idea that the defensiveness itself keeps everything locked in place, so even someone who's genuinely open just thinks 'I'm not getting into that.' Does that land for the rest of you? Henry, Bilal, Connor — does that match anything in your own experience, or does it look different from where you're sitting?

Yeah, I hear what Noah's saying about the defensiveness being self-perpetuating and all that. But I think... I'm not sure it's just about people being defensive for no reason, if that makes sense. Like, I get that it looks like we're all just defending ourselves against an attack that hasn't happened. But I reckon there's something underneath that — it's not just social pressure or people being weird.

It's more about identity, innit? Like, for a lot of blokes, eating meat — especially red meat — that's just part of how you see yourself. It's not conscious most of the time, but it's there. So when someone questions it or steps away from it, it's not just "oh, they made a different choice." It's more like they're questioning something that feels tied to who you are, or what being a bloke means.

I'm not saying that's rational or anything. I'm just saying I don't think the defensiveness is coming from nowhere. It's coming from somewhere real, even if people aren't quite articulating it. It's about masculinity, identity — all that stuff. Not just avoiding conflict or whatever.

That doesn't mean Noah's wrong about it keeping things locked in place or anything. He's probably right about that. But I think if you just see it as defensiveness without understanding why people feel defensive in the first place, you're maybe missing half the picture, you know?

Yeah, okay — fair point. You're right, there's something there about identity that I was kind of skating over. Like, it's not just people being randomly defensive. There's something deeper going on about what it feels like to be a bloke and what that's supposed to mean.

But here's the thing though — and I'm genuinely not sure about this, so I'm kind of thinking out loud — just because I understand why people feel defensive doesn't mean it has to stay like that, does it? Like, yeah, okay, there's this thing where eating meat feels tied up with being a man. I get that. But does that mean we just... accept it? Accept that you can't question it without people getting wound up?

Because that's where it gets a bit embarrassing to me, if I'm honest. Understanding why something happens and then just being like "well, that's how it is" — that feels like we're not really thinking about it properly. 

I don't know what the alternative is, like. I'm not saying I've got it all worked out. But the fact that a dietary choice has become tangled up with what it means to be masculine in the first place — that's kind of a weird thing to just accept as inevitable, isn't it? Even if it makes sense why it happened.

Yeah, that's... that's a fair point, actually. You're right — understanding why something is the way it is doesn't mean it has to stay that way. I wasn't trying to say it's inevitable or anything. Just that it's real, you know?

But now you're saying it, I'm not actually sure. Like, is that identity thing fixed, or is it something that could shift? I don't think I've got a settled answer on that, to be honest. Part of me thinks yeah, people could probably change how they think about it if they wanted to. But another part of me... I don't know. It feels pretty deep, doesn't it? The way being a bloke gets tangled up with what you eat, how you talk about it, all of that.

I guess what I'm saying is — I don't think we should just accept it as how things are, like you're saying. But I'm also not sure how much of it is actually up to us to change, or how much is just... the culture we're all in. Maybe it's both? I don't really know where I land on that yet. But you're right that just shrugging and saying "that's identity" isn't really thinking about it properly.
Henry's landed somewhere a bit uncertain there — 'maybe it's both' — which feels honest. Bilal, Connor, does any of this match what you've seen, or does it look different from where you're sitting?

I think... yeah, Henry's hit on something real there, but I also think — living in London, you'd kind of think this stuff would be looser, wouldn't you? Like, you'd assume that in a big city where nobody really knows anyone, the whole masculine-meat thing would just... dissolve or something. But it doesn't, not really.

I mean, I eat meat regularly, same as all of you. And I don't think I'm under pressure from my mates to do it or anything. But there's this thing where — even when you know intellectually that it shouldn't matter, that it's just a choice — there's still this weight to it. Like, you understand why people get defensive about it. You can see the logic of it coming from somewhere real about identity and how you're raised and what feels normal. But then you're just... living in that anyway, even though you get that it could be different.

That's what gets me about it, actually. I can sit here and think all of this through, understand how it works, see that it's not rational. But when you're actually just living your life day to day, ordering food, going to the supermarket — you're still in that system, you know? It doesn't just dissolve because you've figured out intellectually how it works.

I think that's what Noah's getting at though — just accepting it as how it is doesn't really feel like thinking about it properly. But actually shifting it when you're embedded in the whole thing? That's harder than it sounds. At least it is for me.
Bilal — you've been quiet on this one. Does that match anything in your experience, or does it sit differently for you?

Yeah, I mean... I hear what everyone's saying. But I'm not sure I feel it in the way you're all describing, to be honest.

Like, I eat meat, yeah. I've always eaten meat. But I don't think I feel like it's tied to being a bloke or anything like that. It's just... what I eat. It's convenient, I like it, it's normal to me. I'm not sitting around thinking about my masculinity when I'm having a chicken breast or whatever.

And the thing about people getting defensive — I get that people do that. I've seen it happen. But I'm not sure it's as deep as you're all making it sound. Like, maybe some people do link it to identity, but I don't think everyone does. I think some of us just eat what we eat because we eat it, not because it means something about who we are.

I'm not trying to dismiss what you're saying, but... I genuinely haven't thought about it much, and I'm not sure I buy that it's necessarily wrapped up with masculinity for everyone. It might be for some people, but it feels like you might be reading more into it than what's actually there, if that makes sense.

That's an interesting contrast, Bilal — you're saying it just doesn't carry that weight for you, it's more straightforward than the rest of us have been making it sound. Good to have that in the mix. Okay — we've covered a lot of ground there. Let me move us on, because I want to make sure we get to the next bit. Imagine you actually decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in your life for that to happen?

Yeah, I mean... that's a good question, because I think if I'm being honest, it's not just about the defensiveness thing or the identity stuff. There's practical bits too that I haven't really said yet.

Like, I eat meat most days — chicken, red meat once a week, that sort of thing. And dairy's just... it's in everything for me, isn't it? I have it with breakfast, I'll have cheese, yoghurt. That's a bigger thing than I was saying before, probably. If I had to cut that out, that would actually affect how I eat day to day in a way that would be noticeable.

But more than that — and I think this is the bit I haven't really admitted — I'm just comfortable with how I eat now. It works. I know what to buy, I know how to cook it, it's easy. Going plant-based would mean learning new stuff, working out what actually tastes good, spending time thinking about meals in a way I don't have to now.

And look, I know that's not really a principled reason or anything. It's just... lazy, maybe. But it's true. The defensiveness and the masculinity thing — yeah, that's probably in there somewhere. But honestly, the bigger barrier is just that changing how you eat is a hassle. You'd have to actually think about it, which I don't really do now.

That might sound a bit daft, but it's more honest than pretending it's all about the deep identity stuff, I reckon.

Sam's made a distinction I want to put to the rest of you — he's separating out the identity stuff from something more like just... comfort and habit. Knowing what to buy, knowing how to cook it, not having to think about it. Does that land for any of you? If you imagined actually making that shift, where would the friction actually come from?

Yeah, Sam's hit on something that I think I've been avoiding a bit, to be honest. All the identity stuff — I was talking about it like it's this big thing, but yeah, the actual friction for me? It's more what he said. It's just... comfortable. I know what I'm doing.

I eat chicken most days, red meat once a week, that's just what I do. I know how to cook it, I know where to get it, it takes five minutes. And dairy's the same — cheese on toast, yoghurt in the morning, it's just there. I don't have to think about any of it.

If I went plant-based, I'd have to actually learn stuff. Work out what tastes decent, spend time on it. And I'm not saying there's anything wrong with that — Sam's right, it's not a principled reason. It's just... why would I? I'm not uncomfortable with how I eat now. It works fine.

The masculinity thing, the defensiveness — yeah, maybe that's in there somewhere too. But honestly, the real reason I'm not going plant-based is just because I can't be bothered to change something that already works. That's the truth of it. And I reckon that's probably more real than all the stuff I was saying before about identity and what it means to be a bloke.

Yeah, but I think... I don't know. I hear what you're both saying about the comfort thing, and that's real. But I'm not sure it's as simple as just "can't be bothered," you know?

Like, yeah, there's definitely the practical side — you know how to cook what you eat, you don't have to think about it. That's all true. But I think the comfort itself is doing something deeper than just convenience. It's not just that it's easy. It's that it feels... safe, maybe? Normal in a way that doesn't require you to defend it or explain it or think about it.

Because if it was just about effort, then any hassle would have the same weight, right? But switching to plant-based doesn't feel like switching to a different brand of pasta or something. It feels like... stepping outside of what's expected. And the comfort thing — knowing what to buy, knowing how to cook it — that's partly about it being efficient, sure. But it's also about it being unquestioned. You don't have to justify it.

So when Sam says it's just laziness, I think there's something under that. It's not laziness in a "I can't be bothered" way. It's more like — the comfort of not having to think about it or defend it is kind of the point. And that's wrapped up with the whole masculinity thing Henry was talking about, even if we're not saying it explicitly.

I think what I'm trying to say is — the practical barrier and the identity thing aren't separate, are they? They're kind of the same thing. The comfort works because it's unquestioned. And it's unquestioned because of what we've been talking about all along.

Look, I get what you're saying, Connor, but I think you're kind of... tying it back to the bigger stuff when I wasn't necessarily saying it's all connected like that.

Yeah, maybe some of that defensiveness or the unquestioned thing is in there. But when I said it's just comfort and habit, I meant it — I genuinely don't think about it most days. I buy chicken, I cook it, I eat it. That's not me unconsciously defending my masculinity or feeling safe in the system or whatever. It's just... what I do.

The practical barrier is real, yeah. Learning new recipes, trying stuff, spending time on it — that's a genuine hassle. But that's not the same as saying the comfort is secretly about not having to defend anything. Sometimes comfort is just comfort. You know what works, so you stick with it. That's not necessarily wrapped up in some deeper identity thing.

I'm not saying the masculinity stuff isn't real — I said earlier I think it probably is in there somewhere. But I think I was being more honest when I just admitted I can't be bothered to change something that works fine. That's the actual barrier for me day to day, you know? Not some deep psychological thing about safety and being unquestioned. Just... I'm alright with how I eat now, so why would I?

Fair enough, that's a reasonable pushback. I'm probably overcomplicating it.

But I think there's maybe a difference between "I don't think about it" and "I've stopped thinking about it," you know? Like, you might genuinely not be thinking about it day to day — you're right, you just buy chicken and cook it. That's not the same as consciously defending anything.

But the thing is — you said earlier that you wouldn't order a salad in front of your mates because it would feel a bit off. You remember saying that? That's not "I don't think about it." That's you actively not doing something because of how it would land. And that's only possible if there's something you're already thinking about, even if you're not aware you're thinking about it.

So maybe it's not that the comfort is secretly about defending your masculinity. Maybe it's more that the comfort works *because* you're not questioning it. And the reason you're not questioning it is because you've already absorbed all of that stuff about what's normal and what isn't. Not as some deep identity thing you're protecting consciously, but just as... the water you're swimming in, basically.

I'm not trying to psychoanalyze you or anything. I just think there's a gap between saying "I genuinely don't think about it" and the fact that you're still not ordering something in front of your mates. Those two things don't quite add up, do they?
